DBMS-F-03.question: What do the ACID properties of a transaction mean?
DBMS-F-03.rephrase: A database transaction is said to be ACID. What are those four properties?

key_points.point: Atomicity: all operations happen or none do
Consistency: moves the database from one valid state to another (constraints hold)
Isolation: concurrent transactions do not interfere
Durability: committed changes survive crashes

follow_ups.text: Why is atomicity difficult to guarantee if the server crashes in the middle of a transaction?

key_points.point: Partial writes may already be on disk
Needs a log to undo/redo (rollback)

follow_ups.text: What could go wrong if two transactions were not isolated from each other? Give an example.

key_points.point: Names an anomaly: dirty read, lost update, non-repeatable read, phantom

hints: Imagine transferring 500 rupees from one bank account to another and the power goes off halfway.

misconceptions.text: Consistency means all copies of data are the same (that is replication consistency)

DBMS-F-11.question: What is the difference between DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP?
DBMS-F-11.rephrase: How do DELETE, TRUNCATE and DROP differ in what they remove?

key_points.point: DELETE removes selected rows (WHERE), is DML and can be rolled back
TRUNCATE removes all rows, keeps the table structure, is faster/DDL
DROP removes the whole table including structure

follow_ups.text: Why is TRUNCATE usually much faster than DELETE without a WHERE clause?

key_points.point: Deallocates pages instead of logging each row delete

hints: Think of an exam answer sheet: erasing some answers, erasing all answers, or throwing away the sheet.

DBMS-F-13.question: What is the difference between a shared lock and an exclusive lock?
DBMS-F-13.rephrase: Why do databases have both read locks and write locks?

key_points.point: Shared (read) lock lets many transactions read together
Exclusive (write) lock: only one transaction, no one else reads or writes
Shared locks are compatible with each other; exclusive with none

follow_ups.text: What is two-phase locking, and what does it guarantee?

key_points.point: Growing phase acquires locks, shrinking phase only releases
Guarantees conflict serialisability

hints: Think about a notice board in college: what is safe for many people to do at once, and what isn't?

DBMS-A-02.question: A college fest site sells 500 tickets. During the rush, 520 tickets got sold. The code reads the remaining count, checks it is above zero, and then decrements it. Reason aloud: what went wrong, and how would you fix it?
DBMS-A-02.rephrase: Two buyers both saw one ticket left and both bought it. Why did this happen, and how do you stop it?

key_points.point: Race condition: two transactions read the same value before either updates (lost update)
Make check-and-decrement atomic: conditional UPDATE ... WHERE remaining > 0 and check rows affected
Or lock the row (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE) inside a transaction
Or use serializable isolation / optimistic version check with retry

follow_ups.text: If you lock the row with SELECT FOR UPDATE, what happens to performance during the rush, and is that acceptable here?

key_points.point: Requests queue behind the lock: lower throughput, higher latency
Acceptable because correctness matters; keep transaction short

follow_ups.text: How would you test that your fix actually prevents overselling?

key_points.point: Concurrent/load test with many simultaneous buyers, then check count

hints: Imagine two buyers whose requests reach the server at exactly the same millisecond. Step through what each one sees.

DBMS-F-07.question: Explain the different types of joins: inner join, left outer join and full outer join.
DBMS-F-07.rephrase: How do inner, left and full outer joins differ in the rows they return?

key_points.point: Inner join returns only matching rows from both tables
Left join returns all rows of the left table plus matches, NULLs where no match
Full outer join returns all rows of both tables
Unmatched columns are filled with NULL

follow_ups.text: How would you find students who have not enrolled in any course using a join?

key_points.point: LEFT JOIN enrolments
WHERE enrolment key IS NULL

hints: Picture two overlapping circles, one per table.

DBMS-A-05.question: A payment app moves money from wallet A to wallet B with two separate UPDATE statements and no transaction. Occasionally money disappears. Reason aloud about the causes and design a fix.
DBMS-A-05.rephrase: Money sometimes vanishes when transferring between two wallets using two separate updates. Why, and how would you fix it?

key_points.point: No atomicity: a crash between the updates debits A without crediting B
Wrap both in a single transaction with BEGIN/COMMIT, rollback on failure
Check sufficient balance atomically (WHERE balance >= 500) / constraint
Make retries idempotent (transfer id) to avoid double debit

follow_ups.text: What if wallets A and B live in two different databases? Can one transaction still cover both?

key_points.point: Needs distributed transaction (two-phase commit) or saga with compensation

follow_ups.text: Why might two transfers between the same wallets in opposite directions deadlock, and how can you prevent it?

key_points.point: Each locks one wallet then waits for the other
Always lock rows in a fixed order (e.g. by id)

hints: Think about exactly what state the two balances are in if the server dies at the comment line.

DBMS-D-02.question: Compare the isolation levels read committed, repeatable read and serializable. What does each one allow, and what does it cost?
DBMS-D-02.rephrase: As you go from read committed to serializable, which anomalies disappear, and what do you pay for that?

key_points.point: Read committed: no dirty reads, but non-repeatable reads possible
Repeatable read: same row reads stay the same, phantoms may appear
Serializable: as if transactions ran one after another
Higher isolation costs concurrency/throughput (more locking or aborts)

follow_ups.text: Why don't databases just use serializable everywhere by default?

key_points.point: Throughput falls: more blocking, deadlocks or serialization failures

follow_ups.text: What if an application must be correct for a ticket booking system that may oversell seats? Which level would you choose and why?

key_points.point: Serializable or explicit locking (SELECT ... FOR UPDATE)
Justifies by preventing lost updates/oversell

hints: List the anomalies you know first, then ask which level stops each one.

DBMS-F-04.question: What is normalisation, and why do we normalise a database?
DBMS-F-04.rephrase: Why would a database designer split one big table into several smaller tables?

key_points.point: Organising tables to reduce redundancy (duplicate data)
Avoids insertion, update and deletion anomalies
Done by decomposing tables using functional dependencies / normal forms
Improves data integrity / consistency

follow_ups.text: Give me an example of an update anomaly in an unnormalised table.

key_points.point: Same fact stored in many rows, change missed in some

follow_ups.text: Is there ever a good reason to denormalise? When?

key_points.point: Faster reads / fewer joins for reporting or read-heavy workloads

hints: Think about storing a department's phone number on every employee's row, and then the phone number changes.

misconceptions.text: Normalisation is done to make queries faster

DBMS-D-05.question: How does a query optimiser decide how to execute a SQL query? What information does it use?
DBMS-D-05.rephrase: The same SQL can be executed in many ways. How does the database pick one?

key_points.point: Generates alternative plans (join orders, access methods)
Estimates cost of each plan and picks the cheapest
Uses statistics: table sizes, selectivity, histograms, indexes available
EXPLAIN shows the chosen plan

follow_ups.text: What happens if the table statistics are badly out of date?

key_points.point: Wrong cardinality estimates lead to bad plans (e.g. full scan or wrong join)
Fix with ANALYZE / update statistics

follow_ups.text: Why might the optimiser ignore an index that exists on the filtered column?

key_points.point: Low selectivity: most rows match, so a full scan is cheaper
Function on the column / type mismatch prevents use

hints: Think about how you would choose a route across a city if you had a rough idea of traffic on each road.

DBMS-D-04.question: How does multiversion concurrency control (MVCC) work, and why do databases like PostgreSQL use it?
DBMS-D-04.rephrase: What does it mean for a database to keep multiple versions of a row, and what problem does that solve?

key_points.point: Writers create new row versions instead of overwriting
Readers see a consistent snapshot
Readers don't block writers and writers don't block readers
Old versions must be garbage collected (vacuum)

follow_ups.text: What problem appears if old versions are never cleaned up?

key_points.point: Table bloat, slower scans, wasted storage (transaction ID wraparound)

follow_ups.text: Can two concurrent MVCC transactions still conflict? Give an example.

key_points.point: Write-write conflict on the same row, or write skew

hints: Think about how a library could let one person read an old edition while the new edition is being printed.

DBMS-F-05.question: Explain first, second and third normal form in simple terms.
DBMS-F-05.rephrase: What conditions does a table need to meet to be in 1NF, 2NF and 3NF?

key_points.point: 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups
2NF: 1NF and no partial dependency on part of a composite key
3NF: 2NF and no transitive dependency (non-key depends on non-key)
terms: non key attribute depends on another non key

follow_ups.text: How is BCNF stricter than third normal form?

key_points.point: Every determinant must be a candidate/super key
3NF allows a prime attribute to depend on a non-key

follow_ups.text: Take a table Enrolment(roll_no, course_id, student_name, grade). Which normal form does it violate, and why?

key_points.point: Violates 2NF
student_name depends only on roll_no, part of the key

hints: For each normal form, ask what a non-key column is allowed to depend on.

misconceptions.text: 3NF means a table has exactly three columns or three tables

DBMS-D-01.question: Why do most databases use B+ trees for indexes rather than binary search trees or hash tables?
DBMS-D-01.rephrase: What makes a B+ tree a good fit for database indexes stored on disk?

key_points.point: High fan-out keeps the tree shallow, so few disk reads
Nodes sized to disk pages/blocks
Leaves are linked, so range queries are efficient
Hash tables cannot do range or ordered scans; BSTs are deep/unbalanced

follow_ups.text: Why does the height of the tree matter so much more on disk than in memory?

key_points.point: Each level is a disk/page read, which is orders of magnitude slower than RAM

follow_ups.text: What if your workload were only exact-match lookups on a key, never ranges? Would you still choose a B+ tree?

key_points.point: A hash index could be faster (O(1)) for equality
Trade-off: no ordering, resizing cost

follow_ups.text: What happens inside a B+ tree when you insert into a full leaf node?

key_points.point: Leaf splits into two, middle key pushed to parent
Splits can propagate to the root, increasing height

hints: Think about where an index lives and which kind of access is expensive there.

misconceptions.text: B in B-tree stands for binary

DBMS-F-12.question: How does a database recover after a crash? What role does the log play?
DBMS-F-12.rephrase: After a sudden power failure, how does the DBMS bring the data back to a correct state?

key_points.point: Changes are recorded in a log before data pages (write-ahead logging)
Redo committed transactions
Undo uncommitted transactions
Checkpoints limit how much log must be processed

follow_ups.text: Why must the log record be written to disk before the data page it describes?

key_points.point: Otherwise a crash could leave a change on disk with no way to undo it

follow_ups.text: What is a checkpoint and what problem does it solve?

key_points.point: Point where dirty pages are flushed; recovery starts there instead of the beginning of the log

hints: Think of a diary in which you note down every change before you make it.

DBMS-A-01.question: Here is a slow query on an orders table with ten million rows. It takes eight seconds. Walk me through how you would find out why it is slow and how you would fix it.
DBMS-A-01.rephrase: This query over ten million orders takes eight seconds. How would you investigate and speed it up?

key_points.point: Check the plan with EXPLAIN to see a full table scan
Add an index, ideally composite on (customer_id, created_at)
YEAR() on the column prevents index use; rewrite as a date range
Verify the improvement by measuring again

follow_ups.text: Why does wrapping created_at inside YEAR() stop the database from using an index on created_at?

key_points.point: The index is on raw values; a function result must be computed for every row

follow_ups.text: What if this query is fast now, but inserts into orders have become slower. What trade-off did you make?

key_points.point: Each extra index must be updated on every insert/update
Balance read vs write; drop unused indexes

hints: Before changing anything, what tool would show you how the database is actually running this query?

misconceptions.text: Adding more RAM or a bigger server is the first fix

DBMS-A-01.code_snippet:
SELECT order_id, amount
FROM orders
WHERE YEAR(created_at) = 2025
  AND customer_id = 4821
ORDER BY created_at DESC;

DBMS-D-03.question: What is a lossless-join decomposition, and how do you check that splitting a table did not lose information?
DBMS-D-03.rephrase: When you split a relation into two, how can you be sure joining them gives back exactly the original?

key_points.point: Joining the parts returns exactly the original relation (no spurious tuples)
Common attributes must be a key of at least one part
Dependency preservation is a separate property

follow_ups.text: Why can decomposing to BCNF lose dependency preservation, while 3NF never does?

key_points.point: BCNF splitting may separate attributes of a functional dependency across tables
3NF synthesis keeps every dependency in some table

hints: Think about what the columns shared by the two new tables must look like.

DBMS-A-04.question: This query is supposed to show each department with its number of employees, including departments with no employees. But departments with zero employees are missing. Explain why and how to fix it.
DBMS-A-04.rephrase: Why does this query drop departments that have no employees, and how would you correct it?

key_points.point: Inner JOIN removes departments without matching employees
Use LEFT JOIN from departments
COUNT(e.id) instead of COUNT(*) so empty departments show 0

follow_ups.text: After switching to LEFT JOIN but keeping COUNT(*), what number would an empty department show, and why?

key_points.point: Shows 1, because the NULL-filled row still counts as a row

hints: Ask yourself which rows the JOIN produces for a department that has no employees at all.
DBMS-A-04.code_snippet:
SELECT d.name, COUNT(*) AS staff
FROM departments d
JOIN employees e ON e.dept_id = d.id
GROUP BY d.name;

DBMS-F-10.question: What is a deadlock in a database, and how can it be handled?
DBMS-F-10.rephrase: Two transactions are each waiting for the other to release a lock. What is this called and what can the DBMS do about it?

key_points.point: Two or more transactions wait for each other's locks forever
Detection with a wait-for graph and aborting a victim
Prevention: lock ordering, wait-die/wound-wait, timeouts

follow_ups.text: If the DBMS has to abort one transaction to break a deadlock, how should it choose which one?

key_points.point: Least cost: least work done / fewest locks / youngest
Avoid starving the same transaction repeatedly

hints: Picture two cars meeting in the middle of a narrow one-lane bridge.

misconceptions.text: Deadlock and starvation are the same

DBMS-A-03.question: Design the tables for a library system: members borrow books, a book can have many copies, and we must know who has which copy and when it is due. Talk me through your tables and keys.
DBMS-A-03.rephrase: What tables, columns and keys would you create for a library that tracks members, books, copies and loans?

key_points.point: Separate Book (title-level) and Copy (physical item) tables
Member table with member_id primary key
Loan/borrow table linking member and copy with dates
Foreign keys from Loan to Member and Copy; Copy to Book

follow_ups.text: How would you find all overdue books with your design?

key_points.point: Query loans where due_date < today and return_date IS NULL

follow_ups.text: What if the library now wants to let members reserve a book that is currently out? What changes?

key_points.point: New Reservation table referencing Member and Book (not copy), with date/queue order

hints: Start by listing the real-world things involved. Is 'a book' the same thing as 'the copy on the shelf'?

DBMS-F-06.question: What is the difference between the WHERE clause and the HAVING clause in SQL?
DBMS-F-06.rephrase: When would you filter with HAVING instead of WHERE?

key_points.point: WHERE filters rows before grouping
HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY
HAVING can use aggregate functions; WHERE cannot

follow_ups.text: Write, in words, a query that lists departments having more than five employees.

key_points.point: GROUP BY department
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5

hints: Think about the order in which the database processes the different clauses of a query.

DBMS-W-02.question: To begin, briefly describe a project you have worked on, ideally one that stores or processes data, and explain your role in it.
DBMS-W-02.rephrase: What is one project you worked on, and what did you do in it?

key_points.point: Says what the project does
Mentions data or storage
Explains their own contribution

follow_ups.text: What was the hardest problem you hit in that project, and how did you solve it?

key_points.point: Describes a concrete problem and fix

hints: Tell me a little more: what did it do, what data did it keep, and which part did you build yourself?

DBMS-D-08.question: When would you choose a surrogate key, like an auto-increment ID, instead of a natural key such as a roll number or email?
DBMS-D-08.rephrase: What are the pros and cons of using an artificial ID column as the primary key?

key_points.point: Natural keys can change (email, phone) and break references
Surrogate keys are stable, small and fast to join/index
Still need a unique constraint on the natural key
Surrogate has no business meaning

follow_ups.text: If you use an auto-increment ID, what goes wrong if you forget a unique constraint on email?

key_points.point: Duplicate users/records with the same email can be inserted

hints: Think about ten related tables, four years of data, and what the key column in each of them would hold.

DBMS-F-02.question: Explain super key, candidate key and primary key, and how they are related.
DBMS-F-02.rephrase: What are super keys and candidate keys, and where does the primary key fit in?

key_points.point: Super key: any set of attributes that uniquely identifies a row
Candidate key: a minimal super key
Primary key: the candidate key chosen by the designer
Every candidate key is a super key, not vice versa
terms: every candidate key is a super key
all candidate keys are super keys

follow_ups.text: In a Students table with roll number, email and name, which of these could be candidate keys and why?

key_points.point: Roll number and email (unique)
Name is not unique

hints: Start from the job a key does in a table, then ask whether every column in a key set is really needed.

misconceptions.text: Candidate key and super key are the same thing

DBMS-F-14.question: What is a dirty read? Which isolation level prevents it?
DBMS-F-14.rephrase: What happens when one transaction reads data that another transaction has not yet committed?

key_points.point: Reading data written by an uncommitted transaction
That transaction may roll back, so the value never existed
READ COMMITTED (or higher) prevents it

follow_ups.text: What is a phantom read, and why doesn't row locking alone prevent it?

key_points.point: New rows matching a condition appear on re-query
Needs range/predicate/gap locks or serializable

hints: Imagine you check a friend's bank balance while their deposit is still being processed, and then the deposit fails.

DBMS-F-09.question: What is an entity-relationship diagram, and what are entities, attributes and relationships?
DBMS-F-09.rephrase: What does an ER diagram show, and what are its main building blocks?

key_points.point: Conceptual/visual model of the database design
Entity: a real-world object or concept (rectangle)
Attribute: property of an entity (oval)
Relationship: association between entities (diamond)

follow_ups.text: How would you convert a many-to-many relationship, like students and courses, into tables?

key_points.point: Create a separate junction/bridge table
Holding foreign keys to both, composite primary key

hints: Think of a college office: what does it keep records about, and how are those records related?

DBMS-D-07.question: What is a weak entity? How is it identified and represented in tables?
DBMS-D-07.rephrase: Some entities cannot be identified by their own attributes. How do we model them?

key_points.point: Cannot be uniquely identified by its own attributes
Identified via an owner/strong entity plus a partial key (discriminator)
Table's primary key = owner's key + partial key; total participation

follow_ups.text: Give an example of a weak entity from a college or hospital system.

key_points.point: Concrete example such as dependent of employee, room in building, instalment of loan

follow_ups.text: Why does deleting the owner usually delete the weak entity rows too?

key_points.point: Weak entity has no meaning/identity without its owner

hints: Think of rooms numbered 101, 102 in several different buildings.

DBMS-D-06.question: Explain the steal and no-force policies in buffer management and why they make recovery need both undo and redo.
DBMS-D-06.rephrase: If the database may write uncommitted pages to disk, and need not write committed pages immediately, what does recovery have to do?

key_points.point: Steal: uncommitted changes may be written to disk (needs undo)
No-force: committed changes need not be flushed at commit (needs redo)
Gives better performance/flexibility for the buffer manager
ARIES / write-ahead log provides both

follow_ups.text: What if a system used no-steal and force instead? What would be simpler and what would be worse?

key_points.point: No undo or redo needed (simpler recovery)
But poor performance: forced writes at commit, buffer must hold all uncommitted pages

hints: Ask yourself which pages can be on disk at the moment of a crash under each policy.

DBMS-F-08.question: What is an index in a database and why is it used?
DBMS-F-08.rephrase: Why do databases create indexes on columns?

key_points.point: Data structure that speeds up searching/lookups
Usually a B-tree/B+ tree or hash structure
Costs extra storage and slows inserts/updates
Like the index at the back of a book

follow_ups.text: Why not simply create an index on every column?

key_points.point: Writes become slow because every index must be updated
Extra storage; optimizer may not use them

follow_ups.text: What is the difference between a clustered and a non-clustered index?

key_points.point: Clustered: table rows stored in index order, only one per table
Non-clustered: separate structure with pointers to rows

hints: Think of how you find a topic in a 900-page textbook without reading every page.

DBMS-F-01.question: What is the difference between a primary key and a foreign key?
DBMS-F-01.rephrase: How is a primary key different from a foreign key in a relational table?

key_points.point: Primary key uniquely identifies each row
Primary key cannot be null
Foreign key refers to the primary key of another table
Foreign key enforces referential integrity

follow_ups.text: Can a foreign key column contain NULL values or duplicate values? Why?

key_points.point: Foreign keys may repeat (many-to-one)
NULL allowed unless declared NOT NULL (optional relationship)

follow_ups.text: What happens if you try to delete a row in the parent table that other rows still refer to?

key_points.point: Delete is rejected / restricted
Or ON DELETE CASCADE / SET NULL behaviour

hints: Think of a Students table and an Enrolments table: how does each row in Enrolments know which student it belongs to?

misconceptions.text: A table can have several primary keys
